title: GMAT Data Insights: The Section That Defines Focus Edition
summary: The new third of the GMAT — five question types that test whether you can read data and reason across sources, calculator allowed.

nodes.label: Data Sufficiency
nodes.note: Is the info ENOUGH to answer?

chunks.heading: Why Data Insights matters
chunks.body: Data Insights is **equally weighted** with Quant and Verbal, so it's a full third of your score — no longer an afterthought. It tests **reading, interpreting and combining data** from tables, charts and text to make decisions, and an **on-screen calculator is available** here (unlike Quant).
chunks.realExample: Business schools care about this section because it mirrors real analytics work — turning messy data into a decision. Neglecting it now costs a third of your total score.
chunks.memoryHook: DI = a full third of the score, with a calculator. Never treat it as optional.

chunks.heading: Data Sufficiency — enough, not the answer
chunks.body: Data Sufficiency gives a question plus **two statements**; you decide **whether each alone, both together, or neither is enough to answer** — you usually **don't compute the final answer**. The five choices never change, so learn them cold.
chunks.realExample: 'Is x > 5?' Statement 1: x > 3 (not enough). Statement 2: x = 7 (enough alone). You answer 'statement 2 alone is sufficient' — without needing anything beyond that judgement.
chunks.memoryHook: DS asks 'is it ENOUGH?', not 'what's the answer?'. Judge sufficiency, don't solve.

chunks.heading: Multi-Source & Table — organise before you answer
chunks.body: **Multi-Source Reasoning** spreads information across **tabs** (text, tables, charts) you must combine. **Table Analysis** lets you **sort a table** to judge true/false statements. Both reward a calm, **find-the-relevant-data-first** approach over rushing.
chunks.realExample: In Table Analysis, sorting the column the statement is about (e.g. by revenue) often makes 'the top 3 all exceed X' instantly checkable — use the sort, don't eyeball.
chunks.memoryHook: Sort and locate first. In DI, finding the right data is half the answer.

chunks.heading: Graphics & Two-Part — read the format carefully
chunks.body: **Graphics Interpretation** gives a chart and **dropdown sentences** to complete from it. **Two-Part Analysis** asks for **two answers** (one per column) that together satisfy a condition. Both punish careless reading of the chart or the prompt's exact requirement.
chunks.realExample: In Two-Part Analysis, the two columns might be 'maximises revenue' and 'minimises cost' — a choice can be right for one column and wrong for the other, so read each column's requirement separately.
chunks.memoryHook: Read the chart axes / each column's requirement exactly. DI traps are misreads.

recall.q: How is the Data Insights section weighted, and is a calculator allowed?
recall.a: It's equally weighted with Quant and Verbal (a full third of the score), and an on-screen calculator is available in Data Insights.

recall.q: What does a Data Sufficiency question actually ask?
recall.a: Whether the given statements are sufficient to answer — not what the final answer is.

recall.q: What are the five Data Insights question types?
recall.a: Data Sufficiency, Multi-Source Reasoning, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation and Two-Part Analysis.

recall.q: What's the best approach to Table Analysis?
recall.a: Sort the relevant column first, then judge the true/false statements — don't eyeball the data.

recall.q: What must you watch for in Two-Part Analysis?
recall.a: Each of the two columns has its own requirement, so an option can be right for one and wrong for the other.
